Where it began

Dennis Lillee was born in Perth on 18 July 1949, and Western Australia was his cricket home from the start. He first played for the state in 1969–70, aged 20, and ended that summer as its top wicket-taker.

Within a year he was in the Test side, picked for the last match of the 1970–71 Ashes at Adelaide. He took five wickets in the first innings, which is a fair way to say hello.

The player

Lillee played 70 Tests for Australia between 1971 and 1984 and took 355 wickets at 23.92. He took five in an innings 23 times and ten in a match seven times. His 31 wickets in England in 1972 made his name, and Wisden chose him as a Cricketer of the Year.

An injury in 1973 kept him out for a long spell. He came back with a reworked action and a punishing fitness routine, and in 1974–75 he and Jeff Thomson tore through England's batting together. Later came the Centenary Test of 1977, where his 11 wickets decided the match, and the summer of 1981–82, when his 7 for 83 at the MCG carried him past Lance Gibbs as the leading wicket-taker in Test cricket. In his last Test, at Sydney in January 1984, he took a wicket with his final ball.

What made him special

In his early years he was simply very fast; in 1975 his bowling was timed at 154.8 km/h. As the years went by he shortened his run and leaned on seam movement and cunning, and the wickets kept coming. Few great fast bowlers have changed their method so thoroughly and lost so little.

He also had the perfect partner behind the stumps. The scorecard line "c Marsh b Lillee" appeared 95 times in Tests, more than any other bowler and keeper had managed, and in 1988 the WACA Ground named a grandstand after the pair of them. His batting was more willing than refined, with 905 Test runs at 13.71, but his 73 not out at Lord's in 1975 got Australia out of a tight spot.

Away from the middle

He took a wicket with his first ball on a brief return for Tasmania in 1987–88, then gave years to coaching young fast bowlers, among them Brett Lee, Mitchell Johnson and Pat Cummins. From 2004 to 2015 he was president of the Western Australian Cricket Association.

The honours piled up: an MBE in 1981, the Australian Sports Medal in 2000 and membership of the Order of Australia in 2010. In 1996 he was one of the first ten named to Australia's cricket Hall of Fame; he joined the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame in 2009 and was picked in Australia's Test Team of the Century.

And finally

Not many bowlers turn up in pop songs. Lillee managed two. Lord Kitchener recorded "Water Lillee" in 1976, and Men at Work had their listeners sitting by the television to cheer him on in "No Restrictions". Batsmen of the 1970s may have preferred to watch him that way too.
